title: Hirak Rif Movement Precursors in North
reason: 2012 protests in Morocco's Rif region are well-corroborated: starting March 5, 2012 in Beni Bouayach (Al Hoceima province), a general strike and road blockades triggered escalating confrontations with police that spread to Imzouren, Boukidane, and other Rif towns through March. Grievances cited by protesters and local officials included unemployment (especially among diploma holders), poor water/electricity supply, weak education services, high cost of living, and regional marginalization -- matching the description's 'chronic underdevelopment, high unemployment, marginalisation' framing. These protests were smaller/more localized than the 2011 February 20 Movement wave and are explicitly discussed by academic sources (CIDOB's 'Le temps des cerises' analysis) as a precursor protest cycle to the 2016-2017 Hirak Rif movement. HOWEVER, the specific claim of 'fish vendor protests' in 2012 is not corroborated by any source found. No account of 2012 Rif unrest (Moroccan press, Marxist.com contemporaneous report, academic literature) mentions fish vendors or market vendors as protagonists. The famous fish-vendor-triggered unrest in the Rif is the 2016 death of Mouhcine Fikri (crushed in a garbage truck retrieving confiscated swordfish), which actually launched Hirak Rif -- this appears to be a conflation/anachronistic detail inserted into the 2012 description. Country and year hold, and the general socioeconomic-protest/precursor narrative holds, but the 'fish vendor protests' actor detail is unsubstantiated and likely incorrect, so I'm marking this PARTIAL rather than TRUE.

title: Tanger Med Port Concept Takes Shape
reason: Country and general timeframe hold up: multiple independent sources confirm the Tanger Med deepwater port concept originated in the mid-to-late 1990s under Moroccan planners, with feasibility/site-selection work culminating in the 1999 choice of the Mediterranean location over an Atlantic-coast alternative, and that Mohammed VI (who acceded to the throne in 1999) subsequently gave the project its political push (foundation stone laid 2002, TMSA created 2003, port inaugurated 2007). This substantially matches the description's core narrative of late-1990s feasibility studies followed by post-1999 political momentum. However, the description contains a clear factual error on a named actor: it states "Mohammed V's death in 1999," but Mohammed V (Mohammed VI's grandfather) died in 1961 — it was Hassan II (Mohammed VI's father) who died on 23 July 1999, triggering Mohammed VI's accession. This is a material misattribution of which monarch died in 1999, even though the surrounding causal claim (a royal death in 1999 opening space for Mohammed VI's push on Tanger Med) is otherwise consistent with the historical record. No source pins the feasibility work to the specific year 1998 rather than 1997 or 1999, but "late 1990s" is well corroborated. Given country+year-window hold but a material named-actor detail is wrong, this is a PARTIAL rather than TRUE or FALSE.

title: Tangier Free Zone Established as Export Platform
reason: Multiple independent sources converge on a consistent history of Tangier's free zones, and none place an export-oriented "Tangier Free Zone" in 1988. Morocco's legal framework for export free zones (zones franches d'exportation, ZFE) was created by Law 19-94 (Dahir n°1-95-1, 26 Jan 1995). The specific Tangier export free zone (Tanger-Boukhalef), described by memoireonline.com as "the first export free zone" of its kind in Morocco -- matching the description's textile/garment/light-manufacturing investors and its role as precursor to the later, much larger Tanger Med complex -- was created by decree n°2-96-511 on 10 November 1997 and entered into operation around 1999 (per North South Management / general search summaries: "zone franche de Tanger, entrée en exploitation en 1999"). Earlier Tangier free-zone history (a port free zone from 1961/1962, and an industrial zone from 1970) also does not match 1988. No source found supports an establishment in 1988; the year appears to be wrong by roughly a decade.

title: Security Services Launch Systematic Surveillance of Opposition
reason: The broad narrative is well corroborated by multiple independent sources: Morocco's security apparatus (Sûreté Nationale under Oufkir from 1960, restructured into the CAB1 intelligence service in the early 1960s with CIA/French assistance) targeted the leftist UNFP with surveillance and repression, intensifying after Hassan II's 1961 accession and the contested 1962 constitution, escalating into the July 1963 mass-arrest 'conspiracy' crackdown (100+ UNFP members, 11 death sentences), and feeding directly into the later Years of Lead — this matches the event's core claim (country, approximate year, actor, target, trajectory) closely. However, I could not find any independent source confirming the specific granular tactics claimed — 'telephone tapping, postal interception' as standard tools already in place in 1962, or informants specifically 'placed inside the party and its affiliated trade unions' at that date. These read as plausible but unverified embellishments of an otherwise well-attested repression pattern; several sources instead date the intelligence-service buildup to 1960-61 and the first major documented crackdown to July 1963 rather than 1962 specifically. Country and general year/trajectory hold, but the specific surveillance-method details are unconfirmed, so this is marked PARTIAL rather than TRUE.
